articleHeader.title: Python Modules — Complete Guide
articleHeader.subtitle: A complete, professional guide to Python modules — every import variation, the module search path, module caching, creating custom modules, packages, and how to organize real Python projects.

sections.title: What is a Module in Python?

blocks.text: A module in Python is simply a file containing Python code — functions, classes, variables, or runnable statements — that can be imported and reused in other Python files. Every single .py file you write is automatically a module the moment another file imports it; there is no special syntax or declaration required to "turn a file into a module" — the file itself already is one.

Modules exist to solve one of the oldest problems in software: organizing code so it can be reused without being copy-pasted, and so a large program can be split into smaller, independently understandable, independently testable pieces. Instead of writing every function your program needs in one enormous file, you group related functionality into separate modules — a database.py module for data access, a validators.py module for input checks, a utils.py module for shared helpers — and import exactly what each part of your program needs from each one.

Python's own standard library is itself built almost entirely out of modules — os, sys, json, random, datetime, and hundreds of others are simply Python (and some C) files, organized and shipped with every Python installation, that you import exactly the same way you would import your own code. Understanding modules is therefore not a niche skill — it is the mechanism behind literally every import statement you have ever written.
Every module you import falls into one of three categories, each with a different origin and a different level of trust and stability.

rows: os, sys, math, json, datetime, re
Bundled with the Python interpreter itself
Comes free with every Python installation
Anywhere in your project's file structure
Written directly by you — no installation needed

blocks.text: A special subset of built-in modules — like sys and _thread — are actually compiled directly into the CPython interpreter itself, written in C rather than Python, and are technically distinct from standard library modules that happen to be .py files shipped alongside the interpreter (like json or random). From an import statement's point of view, however, both behave identically — you import them exactly the same way, and the distinction rarely matters in day-to-day code.

sections.title: Every Form of the import Statement

blocks.text: Python offers several distinct ways to bring a module's contents into your current file's namespace, each with a different trade-off between convenience and namespace clarity.

rows: The whole module, as an object
The whole module, under a shorter name
from math import sqrt as square_root
Every public name in the module
sqrt(16), pi, all others directly — discouraged
A sibling module within the same package

blocks.label: import_variations.py
lines: from math import sqrt as square_root
from math import *              # imports everything — avoid in real code

blocks.text: The wildcard form, from module import *, is almost universally discouraged in production code because it silently pulls every public name from that module directly into your current namespace, with no prefix at all — making it impossible to tell, just by reading a line of code, which module a given name actually came from, and creating a real risk of one import silently overwriting a name defined elsewhere in your file.

sections.title: How import Actually Works — The Module Search Path

blocks.text: When Python encounters an import module_name statement, it doesn't search your entire hard drive — it checks a very specific, ordered list of locations called the module search path, stored as a list of strings in sys.path. Python checks each location in order and imports the first matching module it finds; if none match, it raises ModuleNotFoundError.

items.strong: 1. The directory of the running script
items.text: — Python always checks the folder containing the file you actually executed first, so local modules right next to your main script are found immediately.
— Any directories listed in this optional environment variable are checked next, letting you add custom search locations without modifying code.
— The installation-specific folders containing os, sys, json, and every other built-in module that ships with Python.
— Where pip installs third-party packages (numpy, requests, django, etc.), typically inside your virtual environment if one is active.

Key insight: a module's top-level code only ever runs once per program execution, no matter how many different files import it. The very first import triggers full execution and caches the result in sys.modules; every subsequent import anywhere else in the program simply reuses that cached module object instantly.

sections.title: Creating and Importing Your Own Module

blocks.text: Writing your own module requires no special syntax at all — you simply save Python code in a .py file, and any other file in the same directory (or on the module search path) can import it by that filename, without the .py extension.

Everything defined at the top level of shapes.py — variables, functions, and classes — becomes an attribute accessible through shapes.whatever_name once imported. This is exactly how the standard library works too: math.pi and math.sqrt are simply attributes of the math module object, defined at that module's top level.

Every Python module has a special built-in variable called __name__. When a file is run directly (e.g. python shapes.py), Python sets that file's __name__ to the string "__main__". When that same file is instead imported by another module, its __name__ is set to its actual module name (e.g. "shapes") instead.

blocks.label: shapes_with_main.py
lines: # This block ONLY runs when shapes.py is executed directly,
# never when it's imported by another file.

blocks.text: This pattern is extremely common because it lets a single file serve two roles at once: a reusable module and a standalone, runnable script. Library code, quick self-tests, command-line entry points, and demonstration code are all placed inside the if __name__ == "__main__": block specifically so they never execute accidentally as a side effect of someone simply importing the file elsewhere.

sections.title: Modules vs Packages — What's the Difference?

blocks.text: A module is a single .py file. A package is a directory containing multiple modules, organized together, with an optional __init__.py file that marks the directory as importable as a single unit. Packages let you group many related modules under one hierarchical namespace, exactly the way the standard library groups things like os.path or third-party libraries group things like numpy.linalg.

rows: A directory containing modules (and possibly sub-packages)
None — any .py file is a module
The numpy package, containing numpy.linalg, numpy.random, etc.

blocks.text: With this structure, other code can write from myapp.utils import validators or from myapp.utils.formatters import format_date — the dots in the import path directly mirror the folder structure on disk. The __init__.py file (even when left completely empty) signals that a directory should be treated as a package, and its code — if any — runs automatically the first time any module inside that package is imported.
Every imported module automatically carries several special dunder (double-underscore) attributes that describe the module itself — useful for introspection, debugging, and dynamic tooling.

blocks.label: module_attributes.py
lines: print(json.__file__)     # the actual path to json's source file
print(json.__doc__)      # the module's docstring, if it has one
print(dir(json))         # a list of every name defined in the module

items.html: __name__ — The module's own name as a string; equals "__main__" only when the file is run directly, as covered above.
__file__ — The absolute file path the module was loaded from; not present for built-in C modules like sys.
__doc__ — The module's docstring — whatever triple-quoted string, if any, appears at the very top of the file.
__package__ — The name of the package this module belongs to, or an empty string for top-level modules.
dir(module) — Not an attribute itself, but a built-in function that lists every name (functions, classes, variables) defined in the module.

sections.title: Module Caching and Reloading with importlib

blocks.text: As covered in the import flowchart, Python caches every imported module in the sys.modules dictionary, keyed by module name. This is why importing the same module from ten different files in the same program only executes that module's top-level code once — every subsequent import is effectively a dictionary lookup, not a re-execution.

blocks.label: sys_modules_cache.py
lines: print('json' in sys.modules)   # True — already cached after the import above
print(sys.modules['json'] is json)   # True — same object

blocks.text: This caching becomes relevant during interactive development — if you edit a module's source file while it's already loaded in a running interactive session (like a Jupyter notebook or the Python REPL), a plain import module_name won't pick up your changes, because the cached version is reused. The importlib.reload() function exists specifically to force Python to re-execute a module's code and refresh the cached version.

blocks.label: importlib_reload.py
lines: # ... you edit shapes.py in your editor while the session is still running ...
importlib.reload(shapes)   # forces shapes.py to re-execute and refresh

blocks.text: importlib.reload() is a development-time convenience tool and is rarely, if ever, used in production code — in a normal program run from start to finish, every module is naturally imported (and cached) exactly once, which is the correct and expected behaviour.

sections.title: How a Python Project's Modules Fit Together

blocks.text: In a well-organized Python project, modules typically form a layered dependency structure — lower layers contain no dependencies on higher ones, keeping the overall system easy to reason about and test.

A common design goal is to avoid circular imports — where module A imports from module B, and module B also (directly or indirectly) imports from module A — which Python can only partially tolerate and which usually signals that shared logic between the two modules should be extracted into a third, lower-level module that both can depend on instead.
This example shows a realistic small project split across two modules, demonstrating imports, module-level constants, and the __main__ guard together.

blocks.text: Practice This Code — Live Editor

blocks.initialCode:
import math

def circle_stats(radius):
    area = math.pi * radius ** 2
    circumference = 2 * math.pi * radius
    return area, circumference

if __name__ == "__main__":
    area, circumference = circle_stats(7)
    print(f"Ashish's circle -> area: {area:.2f}, circumference: {circumference:.2f}")

blocks.text: These practices help keep modules organized, predictable, and easy for other developers (including future you) to navigate.

items.text: — They make it impossible to tell where a given name came from just by reading the code, and risk silently overwriting existing names.
— A module named validators.py should contain validation logic, not database queries or HTTP handling; mixed responsibilities make modules harder to test and reuse.

items.strong: Always guard runnable code with if __name__ == '__main__':
items.text: — Prevents demonstration code, self-tests, or CLI entry points from executing accidentally when the file is imported elsewhere.

items.strong: Group standard library, third-party, and local imports separately
items.text: — PEP 8 recommends three blocks, each internally alphabetized: standard library first, then third-party packages, then your own local modules.
— A short triple-quoted string at the very top explaining the module's purpose shows up automatically via __doc__ and help().

items.strong: Avoid circular imports by extracting shared code
items.text: — If two modules need to import from each other, move the shared logic into a third, lower-level module both can depend on instead.

items.strong: Use packages (with __init__.py) once a project grows past a handful of files
items.text: — A flat pile of unrelated .py files becomes hard to navigate; grouping related modules into packages keeps structure legible as a project scales.

items.strong: Never rely on module-level mutable state across imports without care
items.text: — Since a module's code runs only once and is cached, any mutable global variable it defines is genuinely shared and mutated by every part of the program that imports it.

sections.title: Advantages and Disadvantages of Python's Module System

blocks.text: Python's module system is simple and powerful, but understanding its trade-offs helps you structure larger projects correctly from the start.

pros.title: Zero Boilerplate to Create a Module
pros.text: Any .py file is automatically a valid, importable module — no declarations, headers, or special syntax required.

pros.title: Automatic Caching via sys.modules
pros.text: A module's top-level code runs only once no matter how many times it's imported, keeping large programs efficient.

pros.title: Clean, Hierarchical Namespacing
pros.text: Packages let related modules be grouped and accessed through readable dotted paths like myapp.utils.validators.

pros.title: Massive, Ready-Made Standard Library
pros.text: Hundreds of built-in modules cover file I/O, networking, data formats, and more, without installing anything extra.

pros.title: Encourages Reusable, Testable Code
pros.text: Splitting logic into focused modules makes each piece easier to unit test and reuse across different projects.

pros.title: The __main__ Guard Enables Dual-Purpose Files
pros.text: A single file can act as both an importable library and a standalone runnable script, without conflict.

cons.title: Circular Imports Can Cause Real Problems
cons.text: Two modules importing from each other can raise ImportError or produce partially-initialized modules, depending on import order.

cons.title: Wildcard Imports Hurt Readability
cons.text: from module import * obscures where names actually come from and risks silent name collisions.

cons.title: Module-Level Mutable State Is Shared Everywhere
cons.text: A mutable global variable defined in a module is the same object across every part of the program that imports it, which can cause subtle bugs if not managed carefully.

cons.title: sys.path Search Can Be Confusing for Beginners
cons.text: Understanding why an import succeeds or fails often requires knowing exactly what's in sys.path, which isn't always obvious.

cons.title: Relative Imports Have Quirky Rules
cons.text: Relative imports (from . import x) only work properly inside a recognized package, which trips up beginners running a script directly instead of as part of a package.

blocks.text: Frequently asked interview questions about Python modules, packages, and the import system.

items.q: Q1. What is a module in Python?
items.a: A module is simply a .py file containing Python code — functions, classes, or variables — that can be imported and reused elsewhere. Any Python file is automatically a valid module the moment another file imports it; no special declaration is needed.

items.q: Q2. What is the difference between a module and a package?
items.a: A module is a single .py file. A package is a directory containing multiple related modules (and possibly sub-packages), typically marked with an __init__.py file. Packages let you organize many modules under a hierarchical, dotted namespace like myapp.utils.validators.

items.q: Q3. What is sys.path and how does Python use it during import?
items.a: sys.path is a list of directory paths that Python searches, in order, whenever an import statement runs. It includes the directory of the running script, any PYTHONPATH entries, the standard library location, and the site-packages directory. Python imports the first matching module found while walking this list, and raises ModuleNotFoundError if nothing matches.

items.q: Q4. Why does a module's top-level code only run once, even if imported from multiple files?
items.a: Because Python caches every imported module in the sys.modules dictionary, keyed by its name. The first import executes the module's code and stores the resulting module object in this cache; every subsequent import anywhere else in the same program simply retrieves that same cached object instead of re-executing the file.

items.q: Q5. What does if __name__ == '__main__': actually check?
items.a: It checks whether the current file's built-in __name__ variable equals the string '__main__', which Python sets automatically only when that file is the one being run directly (e.g. python script.py). When the same file is instead imported by another module, __name__ is set to the module's own name instead, so code inside this block never runs during an import.

items.q: Q6. Why is 'from module import *' generally discouraged?
items.a: It imports every public name from the module directly into the current namespace with no prefix, making it impossible to tell from the code alone which module a given name came from. It also risks silently overwriting an existing name in your file if the wildcard import happens to define something with the same name.

items.q: Q7. What is the purpose of the __init__.py file in a package?
items.a: It marks a directory as a Python package, allowing it to be imported as a single unit (e.g. import myapp). Since Python 3.3, packages can technically work without it (as 'namespace packages'), but including __init__.py — even empty — remains common practice, and any code placed inside it runs automatically the first time the package is imported.

items.q: Q8. What is a circular import, and why is it a problem?
items.a: A circular import occurs when module A imports from module B, and module B also imports (directly or indirectly) from module A. Because each module only partially finishes executing before the other tries to import from it, this can raise ImportError or result in a module object that's only partially initialized. The usual fix is extracting the shared logic into a third module both can depend on.

items.q: Q9. What is the difference between an absolute import and a relative import?
items.a: An absolute import specifies the full path from the top-level package, e.g. from myapp.utils import validators. A relative import uses leading dots to reference modules relative to the current module's location within a package, e.g. from . import validators (same package) or from .. import config (parent package). Relative imports only work inside a properly recognized package, not in standalone scripts.

items.q: Q10. How would you force Python to re-import a module that has already been cached?
items.a: Using importlib.reload(module_object), which forces the module's code to re-execute and refreshes the cached version in sys.modules. This is primarily a development-time tool used in interactive sessions like Jupyter or the REPL; it's rarely needed in a normal program that runs start to finish, since a fresh import naturally happens only once per run anyway.

blocks.text: Work through these practice questions on Python modules and the import system. Try to reason through each before checking the answer.

items.q: 1. If module_a.py is imported by three different files in the same running program, how many times does its top-level code actually execute?
items.a: Only once. The first import executes module_a's code fully and stores the resulting module object in sys.modules. Every later import of module_a anywhere else in the same program simply reuses that cached object instead of re-running the file's code.

items.q: 2. What is printed if utils.py contains print('loading utils') at its top level, and it is imported by two different files run in the same program?
items.a: 'loading utils' is printed exactly once, at the very first import — not twice. This directly demonstrates that module code executes only on the first import, with every subsequent import elsewhere in the same run reusing the cached module.

items.q: 3. What is the value of __name__ inside greet.py when it is run directly with 'python greet.py', versus when it is imported by another file as 'import greet'?
items.a: When run directly, __name__ equals '__main__'. When imported by another file, __name__ equals 'greet' (the module's own name) instead. This difference is exactly what the if __name__ == '__main__': pattern relies on.

items.q: 4. Why might 'from . import helpers' fail with an ImportError when a file inside a package is executed directly as a script, but work fine when that same package is imported normally?
items.a: Relative imports (using leading dots) rely on Python knowing the current module's position within a package hierarchy, which is only established when the module is imported as part of that package. Running the file directly as a standalone script sets its __name__ to '__main__' with no package context, so Python cannot resolve the relative import and raises an error.

items.q: 5. Two modules, models.py and services.py, each try to import from the other at the top of their files. What problem does this create?
items.a: This is a circular import. Whichever module is imported first will, partway through its own execution, try to import the second module — but the second module will, in turn, try to import back from the first module, which hasn't finished executing yet and may not yet have all its names defined. This typically raises an ImportError or produces a partially initialized module object.

items.q: 6. What is the output order if config.py defines DEBUG = True at the top level, and two different files both do 'from config import DEBUG' and then modify their own local DEBUG variable?
items.a: Each file's local DEBUG variable becomes an independent copy of the boolean value at the moment of import — modifying one file's local DEBUG does not affect the other, because 'from module import name' binds a new local name to whatever the module's attribute pointed to at that instant. This differs from 'import config; config.DEBUG = False', which does mutate the shared module object itself.

items.q: 7. Does sys.path include the directory of the script you're currently running?
items.a: Yes — Python automatically includes the directory containing the script being executed as the first entry in sys.path, which is why modules placed right next to your main script are found without needing any special configuration.

items.q: 8. What is the practical difference between 'import json' and 'from json import loads'?
items.a: 'import json' brings in the whole module as a single object, requiring the json. prefix for every use (json.loads(...)). 'from json import loads' imports only that one function directly into the current namespace, letting you call it as loads(...) without any prefix — but it makes it slightly less obvious, when reading unrelated code later, exactly which module loads came from.

sections.title: Conclusion — Structuring Python Code with Modules

blocks.text: Modules are the foundation Python's entire code organization system is built on — from the standard library, to every third-party package on PyPI, to your own project's files. Understanding how import actually works, from the module search path through to caching in sys.modules, demystifies behaviour that otherwise seems almost magical: why a module's print statements only ever run once, why editing a file mid-session doesn't automatically update an already-imported module, and why circular imports fail in ways that can be confusing without this mental model.

The most valuable habits to carry forward: keep each module focused on one clear responsibility, guard runnable code with if __name__ == "__main__": so it never executes as a side effect of importing, avoid wildcard imports so every name's origin stays traceable, and reach for packages once a project grows beyond a handful of loosely related files, so its structure stays legible as it scales.

items.q: What is the difference between a module and a library in Python?
items.a: A module is a single .py file. A library (or package) is typically a collection of modules distributed together, often installed via pip, that provide related functionality — for example, the 'requests' library is actually a package containing multiple modules working together. In everyday conversation the terms are sometimes used loosely, but technically a module is the basic building block and a library/package is a collection of them.

items.q: Do I need to install Python's built-in modules like os or json separately?
items.a: No. Standard library modules like os, sys, json, random, and datetime are bundled directly with every Python installation and are available immediately via import, with no pip install step required. Only third-party packages (numpy, requests, django, etc.) need to be installed separately using pip.

items.q: Why does my module-level print statement only run once even though I import it in multiple files?
items.a: Python caches every imported module in the sys.modules dictionary after its first import. The module's top-level code, including any print statements, executes exactly once during that first import; every later import elsewhere in the same running program reuses the already-cached module object instead of re-executing the file.

items.q: What does __name__ == '__main__' actually mean in Python?
items.a: Python automatically sets a file's built-in __name__ variable to the string '__main__' only when that file is the one being executed directly, such as running 'python script.py' from the command line. When the same file is instead imported by another module, __name__ is set to that module's own name. Checking this condition lets you write code that only runs when the file is executed directly, not when it's imported.

items.q: What is the correct way to organize a Python project with multiple modules?
items.a: Group related modules into packages (directories with an __init__.py file), keep each individual module focused on one clear responsibility, avoid circular dependencies between modules, and use a clear main entry point (often main.py) guarded by if __name__ == '__main__':. As a project grows, separating concerns like models, services, and utilities into their own modules or sub-packages keeps the codebase navigable.

items.q: Is 'from module import *' ever acceptable to use in Python?
items.a: It's occasionally seen in small interactive scripts, Jupyter notebooks, or specific libraries explicitly designed for it (some plotting or numerical libraries document this pattern), but it's almost always discouraged in application and library code. It obscures where each imported name actually came from and risks silently overwriting existing names in your namespace, which makes debugging significantly harder in larger codebases.
